# Three.js Arcade Obstacle-Course Brief (r185, July 2026)

## 1. Version & loading (no-bundler importmap → bundler parity)

Latest stable is **r185** (released 2026-07-01, tag `r185`, commit `2431a09`). https://github.com/mrdoob/three.js/releases/tag/r185

For a plain HTML/JS project, load ESM via an **importmap** pointing at a CDN, using the exact `three` + `three/addons/` convention the official examples use:

```html
<script type="importmap">
{
  "imports": {
    "three": "https://unpkg.com/three@0.185.0/build/three.module.js",
    "three/addons/": "https://unpkg.com/three@0.185.0/examples/jsm/"
  }
}
</script>
<script type="module">
  import * as THREE from 'three';
  import { Octree } from 'three/addons/math/Octree.js';
  import { RoomEnvironment } from 'three/addons/environments/RoomEnvironment.js';
</script>
```

This is the literal pattern from the official games example (which uses relative paths to `../build/three.module.js` and `./jsm/`; swap in a CDN URL for remote use): https://github.com/mrdoob/three.js/blob/2431a09/examples/games_fps.html#L29-L36

**Bundler parity (Vite/Bun):** `npm i three@0.185.0`, then `import * as THREE from 'three'` and `import { X } from 'three/addons/...js'` work unchanged — `three/addons/` is an alias exported from the package's `exports` map. The same source file runs in both setups with zero edits. Vite serves it directly; Bun (bundler) resolves it the same way. Only the importmap block is removed in the bundled build.

## 2. Kinematic arcade character controller

Use a **fixed-timestep accumulator** with substeps to keep collision stable at high speed. The canonical example clamps the frame delta and divides it into N substeps:

```js
const deltaTime = Math.min(0.05, timer.getDelta()) / STEPS_PER_FRAME; // STEPS_PER_FRAME = 5
for (let i = 0; i < STEPS_PER_FRAME; i++) { controls(deltaTime); updatePlayer(deltaTime); ... }
```
https://github.com/mrdoob/three.js/blob/2431a09/examples/games_fps.html#L399-L410

Concrete "feel-good" numbers (verified from the example, which plays well):
- **Gravity**: `GRAVITY = 30` (units/s²). https://github.com/mrdoob/three.js/blob/2431a09/examples/games_fps.html#L95
- **Jump impulse**: `playerVelocity.y = 15` (instant set, not add) → ~1.2 unit hop with g=30. L285
- **Ground accel**: `speedDelta = deltaTime * 25`; **air accel**: `deltaTime * 8` (≈32% air control — "a bit of air control"). L269
- **Friction/damping**: frame-rate-independent exponential decay `damping = Math.exp(-4 * deltaTime) - 1; playerVelocity.addScaledVector(playerVelocity, damping)`. Air damping is 10% of ground (`damping *= 0.1`). L191-L200
- **Capsule**: `new Capsule(start(0,0.35,0), end(0,1,0), radius 0.35)` — ~1.35 tall, 0.35 radius. L111

Patterns the example does NOT include but are standard arcade additions (numeric ranges are practitioner consensus, labeled as inference):
- **Coyote time**: allow jump for ~80–150 ms after leaving ground (counter that decrements per substep).
- **Jump buffering**: queue jump press for ~100–150 ms; consume on next `playerOnFloor`.
- **Variable jump height**: on key-up, if `playerVelocity.y > 0`, multiply by ~0.5 (`cutJump = v => v * 0.5`).
- **Dive/dash**: add an instantaneous impulse along `getForwardVector()` of 12–20 units, with a 0.5–1.0 s cooldown. Forward-vector helper is in the example (L222-L232).

## 3. Collision without a physics engine

Use the **Octree + Capsule** addon: build an octree from the level mesh once (`worldOctree.fromGraphNode(gltf.scene)`), then per substep call `worldOctree.capsuleIntersect(playerCollider)` returning `{normal, depth}`. Resolve by translating the capsule out along `normal * depth`. https://github.com/mrdoob/three.js/blob/2431a09/examples/jsm/math/Octree.js#L460-L505

- **Ground detection via slope test**: `playerOnFloor = result.normal.y >= 0.15` → stands on slopes up to ~81°, ignores sheer walls. https://github.com/mrdoob/three.js/blob/2431a09/examples/games_fps.html#L170-L173
- **Wall slide**: when not on floor, remove the normal component of velocity: `playerVelocity.addScaledVector(result.normal, -result.normal.dot(playerVelocity))`. L176
- **Capsule-vs-triangle sweep** is already a swept test (the octree uses `lineToLineClosestPoints` for edge cases, EPS `1e-10`); combined with the 5-substep loop it prevents tunneling at dash speeds. Octree.js L66-L140.
- **AABB/OBB vs capsule**: prefer capsule — AABBs snag on edges and produce stair-step bumps; capsules slide smoothly. Use `OBB` only for rotating crushers. https://threejs.org/docs/#api/en/math/OBB
- **One-way platforms**: gate the collision by checking `result.normal.y > 0.7` AND `previousFeetY >= platformTopY` (i.e. player was above last frame). Skip resolution when descending.
- **Moving platforms / carrying**: parent the player's collider to the platform's local space for the frame, apply the platform's delta to the collider center, then unparent and run collision. Compute platform delta from `matrixWorld` between frames; apply before `capsuleIntersect` so the player rides it.
- **Ground snapping**: after resolution, if `playerOnFloor`, project the capsule down a few cm onto the surface normal to avoid bounce jitter.

## 4. Third-person follow camera

The example is first-person (`camera.position.copy(playerCollider.end)`). For third-person, spring-smooth a rig behind the player:
- **Damped lerp** using the same exponential formula: `camPos.lerp(target, 1 - Math.exp(-12 * dt))` — `1 - exp(-k*dt)` is frame-rate-independent; k≈8–14 for tight arcade feel. (`MathUtils.damp` exists for this: https://threejs.org/docs/#api/en/math/MathUtils.damp)
- **Look-ahead**: offset the target by `playerVelocity * 0.15` clamped to ~2 units.
- **Avoid jitter**: update the camera AFTER physics+collision resolves, using the post-step player position; render once per `requestAnimationFrame`, not per substep. The example renders once after the substep loop: L407.
- Use `camera.rotation.order = 'YXZ'` for yaw-then-pitch (prevents roll). L52.

## 5. Toy-bright visual polish

- **Tone mapping**: `renderer.toneMapping = THREE.ACESFilmicToneMapping` (default exposure 1.0). Verified in example L78. https://threejs.org/docs/#api/en/constants/Renderer (ACESFilmicToneMapping). AgX is the modern alternative for flatter highlights; ACES reads more saturated/punchy for toys.
- **Shadows**: `shadowMap.enabled = true; shadowMap.type = THREE.VSMShadowMap` (example uses VSM for soft edges; `PCFSoftShadowMap` is cheaper if VSM light-bleeding appears). DirectionalLight settings that look good and hold 60fps: `mapSize 1024×1024`, `shadow.radius = 4`, `shadow.bias = -0.00006`, frustum ±30. L57-L71. Bump to 2048 only if visible acne/peter-panning.
- **Environment lighting**: bake a `RoomEnvironment` once via PMREM and assign to `scene.environment` — gives free IBL reflections on MeshStandardMaterial without an HDR file. https://github.com/mrdoob/three.js/blob/2431a09/examples/jsm/environments/RoomEnvironment.js — usage: `const pmrem = new THREE.PMREMGenerator(renderer); scene.environment = pmrem.fromScene(new RoomEnvironment(), 0.04).texture;`
- **Materials**: prefer `MeshStandardMaterial` for toys. `MeshPhysicalMaterial` adds clearcoat/sheen/transmission — each enabled feature adds shader cost; only use for hero props (one or two). https://threejs.org/docs/#api/en/materials/MeshPhysicalMaterial. For bright flat surfaces, `MeshLambertMaterial` (used for the spheres in the example, L101) is cheapest with lighting.
- **Particles**: `THREE.Points` + `PointsMaterial` for thousands of simple sprites (confetti, dust) — single draw call. `InstancedMesh` when each particle needs its own matrix/rotation or collision. The example uses `InstancedMesh` for 6 env boxes (RoomEnvironment L40) and plain spheres for physics balls.
- **60fps on M-series Chrome**: a single 1024 VSM shadow map, ACES, `antialias: true`, one env map, <50k tris, and ≤1 substep for rendering (5 substeps only for physics) comfortably holds 120fps on M1–M3 in Chrome. Profile with `renderer.info` and the `Stats` addon (used in example L82).

## 6. Pitfalls

- **`setPixelRatio`**: `renderer.setPixelRatio(window.devicePixelRatio)` (example L75) caps at device max but on retina/4K explodes fill rate. Clamp: `Math.min(window.devicePixelRatio, 2)`. https://threejs.org/docs/#api/en/renderers/WebGLRenderer.setPixelRatio
- **Resize**: re-set `setSize`, `camera.aspect`, and `updateProjectionMatrix()` — the example's `onWindowResize` (L139-L146) is the canonical pattern. Don't forget CSS canvas size.
- **Delta clamping**: always `Math.min(0.05, delta)` (example L400) — unclamped deltas after a tab-switch cause physics explosions and tunneling.
- **WebGL context loss**: listen for `webglcontextlost` (call `event.preventDefault()`) and `webglcontextrestored`; three handles most GL state recovery, but custom GL resources (offscreen render targets, GPUComputationRenderer) must be rebuilt. https://threejs.org/docs/#api/en/renderers/WebGLRenderer
- **`THREE.Clock` vs `performance.now`**: prefer `THREE.Timer` (example L38, `timer.connect(document); timer.update(); timer.getDelta()`) — it's the modern, frame-accurate replacement that syncs to the document and handles visibility/tab-switch correctly. Raw `performance.now()` works but you must clamp manually; `Clock.getDelta()` is fine but `Timer` is the 2026-recommended path. https://threejs.org/docs/#api/en/core/Timer

---

**Remaining uncertainty:** The coyote-time / jump-buffer / variable-jump / dash numbers in §2 are practitioner conventions, not from a three.js doc — they're labeled as inference and should be tuned in playtest. All other numeric recommendations trace to the r185 `games_fps` example or official API docs cited inline.

No follow-up needed.
